primitives.name: Geometric unification: one symmetry framework underlies CNNs, RNNs, GNNs and Transformers, in the spirit of the Erlangen Programme
primitives.verbatim_quote: Throughout our exposition, we will describe these models, as well as many others, as natural instances of the same underlying principle of geometric regularity.
assumptions: Successful architectures share exploitable geometric regularity rather than being independent inventions.
A common mathematical language of domains, groups and representations can describe all of them.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The unification covers representation learning architectures; the text explicitly excludes pipelines such as generative modelling, reinforcement learning and optimisation methods (Adam, dropout, batch normalisation) from its scope.

layer2.mapping: The engine treats every data source as a signal on a named domain with a named symmetry group, and classifies every model component by that pair, so architectures are compared by the equivalences they respect rather than by surface form.
layer2.telemetry: Domain and group declarations per data source; architecture inventory tagged by domain and group.

primitives.name: Learning requires a regularity prior: among interpolants, choose the most regular under a complexity measure
primitives.verbatim_quote: A successful learning scheme thus needs to encode the appropriate notion of regularity or inductive bias for f , imposed through the construction of the function class F and the use of regularisation.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.R(f-tilde): expected risk of the estimator under distribution P
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: data distribution over X x Y
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: unknown target function generating the labels
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f-tilde: estimated function from the hypothesis class

assumptions: Labels are generated by an unknown function f with y_i = f(x_i) in the noise-free idealisation.
A complexity measure c on the hypothesis class captures the expected regularity of f.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Universal approximation alone gives no generalisation guarantee: with no complexity measure matched to the task, the interpolant is arbitrary among infinitely many candidates, and test risk is uncontrolled.

layer2.mapping: Every engine estimator carries an explicit prior: the hypothesis class and its complexity penalty are declared, and model selection is the search for the most regular explanation of observed data rather than the best memorisation of it.
layer2.telemetry: Declared priors per model; complexity penalty values; out-of-sample risk estimates.

primitives.name: Curse of dimensionality: with only Lipschitz regularity, the required sample count is exponential in dimension
primitives.verbatim_quote: signaling that the Lipschitz class grows ‘too quickly’ as the input dimension increases: in many applications with even modest dimension d, the number of samples would be bigger than the number of atoms in the universe.
assumptions: The target function is only known to be 1-Lipschitz in the input norm.
The domain is a d-dimensional Euclidean domain of diameter 1, so an epsilon-net has size growing as epsilon^{-d}.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The barrier is escaped only by extra structure (symmetry, low-dimensional projections, scale separation); a Sobolev smoothness order s helps only when s grows proportionally to d, which the text calls unrealistic in practice.

layer2.mapping: Sample budgets in the engine are computed against effective dimension after symmetry reduction, not raw feature count; a signal family whose only known regularity is smoothness is flagged as data-starved by construction.
layer2.telemetry: Feature dimensionality per signal; sample counts per regime; symmetry reduction factors.

primitives.name: A symmetry is a transformation that leaves a certain property of the object or system unchanged
primitives.verbatim_quote: Informally, a symmetry of an object or system is a transformation that leaves a certain property of said object or system unchanged or invariant.
assumptions: The property to be preserved is fixed by the task (object category under shifts; molecular property under rotations).
Transformations may be smooth, continuous, or discrete.
primitives.breakdown_regime: If the preserved property is misidentified, the imposed symmetry destroys task-relevant information: reflections are valid symmetries for microscope slides but change the meaning of road signs.

layer2.mapping: Each engine task declares the property that must be preserved, meaning its prediction target, and the transformations under which it is unchanged; those declarations are the symmetry specification every downstream operator is audited against.
layer2.telemetry: Task target definitions; declared transformation sets per task.

primitives.name: The symmetries of an object form a group: associative composition, a unique identity, and inverses
primitives.verbatim_quote: Associativity: (gh)k = g(hk) for all g, h, k ∈ G. Identity: there exists a unique e ∈ G satisfying eg = ge = g for all g ∈ G.
primitives.latex: (gh)k = g(hk), \quad eg = ge = g, \quad gg^{-1} = g^{-1}g = e

symbol_and_unit_ledger.gh: composition, read right to left (apply h, then g)

assumptions: Composition of two symmetries is again a symmetry (closure).
Every symmetry is invertible and its inverse is a symmetry.
Commutativity is not assumed; groups with gh = hg for all elements are the special Abelian case.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Approximate symmetries fail the axioms: small deformations compose into large ones, violating closure, so they cannot be treated as a group and require the deformation stability formalism instead.

layer2.mapping: The engine composes declared transformations algebraically: pipelines of relabellings, reflections and resamplings are checked for closure and invertibility before use, and any non-invertible step is marked as information-destroying.
layer2.telemetry: Transformation pipeline definitions; invertibility flag per step.

primitives.name: Group representation: rho(gh) = rho(g)rho(h) lifts abstract group actions to linear maps on signals
primitives.verbatim_quote: A n-dimensional real representation of a group G is a map ρ : G → Rn×n , assigning to each g ∈ G an invertible matrix ρ(g), and satisfying the condition ρ(gh) = ρ(g)ρ(h) for all g, h ∈ G.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho: representation map from the group G into n x n invertible matrices
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(g): matrix acting on the feature (signal) space
symbol_and_unit_ledger.n: dimension of the representation space, in practice the feature dimension

assumptions: The action on signals is linear in the signal: g.(a x + b x') = a (g.x) + b (g.x').
For infinite domains rho(g) is an operator on an infinite-dimensional signal space and must be discretised for computation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A representation is only as useful as its dimension and fidelity: features must be assigned the representation they actually transform under, and unitary or orthogonal representations are the ones that preserve norms.

layer2.mapping: Engine features are stored with the representation under which they transform, so an operator consuming them can verify it is combining quantities that transform compatibly instead of mixing frames silently.
layer2.telemetry: Per-feature transformation type (scalar, vector, tensor); representation labels per feature block.

primitives.name: G-invariance: f(rho(g)x) = f(x); the function output is unaffected by the group action on the input
primitives.verbatim_quote: A function f : X (Ω) → Y is G-invariant if f (ρ(g)x) = f (x) for all g ∈ G and x ∈ X (Ω), i.e., its output is unaffected by the group action on the input.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: function from signals X(Omega) to outputs Y
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(g): representation of group element g acting on the input signal

assumptions: The task output is genuinely unchanged by every g in G.
The representation rho correctly implements the group action on signals, (g.x)(u) = x(g^{-1} u).
primitives.breakdown_regime: A purely linear G-invariant function is degenerate: it depends on x only through its group average A x, so rich invariance must be built by composing equivariant layers with a final invariant pooling, never by a single linear map.

layer2.mapping: Final engine outputs such as predictions and rankings are required to be invariant under the declared symmetries of the input: relabelling or mirroring the same situation must return the same prediction, and this is tested directly.
layer2.telemetry: Invariance test results per model; symmetry-augmented evaluation sets.

primitives.name: G-equivariance: the group action on the input produces the same action on the output (CNN layers are shift-equivariant, not shift-invariant)
primitives.verbatim_quote: If we however take a closer look at the convolutional layers of CNNs, we will find that they are not shift-invariant but shift-equivariant: in other words, a shift of the input to a convolutional layer produces a shift in the output feature maps by the same amount.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(g), output side: representation on the output space, possibly a different representation of the same group

assumptions: Input and output domains both carry actions of the same group G.
Intermediate features, not only final outputs, should track the transformation.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Exact equivariance to very large groups is unaffordable (the permutation group Sigma_n has n! elements), so practical equivariant layers work through actions on low-dimensional domains rather than over the group itself.

layer2.mapping: Intermediate engine representations stay equivariant: when an input situation is transformed, for example sides swapped or the field mirrored, every intermediate feature map transforms in the matching way, so no layer silently assumes a canonical orientation.
layer2.telemetry: Per-layer equivariance checks; mirrored-input consistency tests.

primitives.name: Isomorphism versus automorphism: equivalence between two distinct objects is not the same notion as a symmetry of one object
primitives.verbatim_quote: To understand the difference, consider a set Ω = {0, 1, 2}. An automorphism of the set Ω is a bijection τ : Ω → Ω such as a cyclic shift τ (u) = u + 1 mod 3. Such a map preserves the cardinality property, and maps Ω onto itself. If we have another set Ω0 = {a, b, c} with the same number of elements, then a bijection η : Ω → Ω0 such as η(0) = a, η(1) = b, η(2) = c is a set isomorphism.
assumptions: Both maps are invertible and structure-preserving at a fixed level of structure.
An automorphism maps an object to itself; an isomorphism maps between two different objects of the same structure.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The distinction shifts with the level of structure: adding structure shrinks the symmetry group (Euclidean isometries E(2) sit inside diffeomorphisms, SE(2) inside E(2)), so what counts as the same depends on the structure chosen.

layer2.mapping: The engine separates two questions that are often confused: whether two situations are the same situation relabelled, in which case outputs must match exactly, and whether one situation corresponds to a genuinely different one, which needs a map between their function spaces rather than between their points.
layer2.telemetry: Situation identity resolution; cross-domain correspondence records.

primitives.name: Deformation stability: replace exact invariance with the bound ||f(rho(tau)x) - f(x)|| <= C c(tau) ||x||
primitives.verbatim_quote: We can now replace our previous definition of exact invariance and equivarance under group actions with a ‘softer’ notion of deformation stability (or approximate invariance):

symbol_and_unit_ledger.c(tau): deformation cost, equal to 0 exactly when tau lies in the symmetry subgroup G
symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: constant independent of the signal x
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(tau): action of the deformation on signals

assumptions: A deformation cost c can be defined with c(tau) = 0 on the symmetry subgroup, e.g. the Dirichlet energy measuring elasticity for images.
Deformations of interest lie near the symmetry subgroup.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The guarantee is only as good as the cost: large deformations can change semantic content, and a cost that mismeasures change away from the subgroup gives vacuous stability; small deformations do not form a group, so exact invariance to them cannot even be stated.

layer2.mapping: Engine comparisons across contexts use stability rather than identity: a model evaluated on a perturbed situation is expected to move its output at most in proportion to a declared perturbation cost, and larger movement is treated as a model defect, not as new information.
layer2.telemetry: Perturbation cost per context shift; measured output drift under perturbation.

primitives.name: Convolution Theorem: convolution in the signal domain is the pointwise product of Fourier transforms
primitives.verbatim_quote: a fact known in signal processing as the Convolution Theorem.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.*: convolution (cross-correlation convention used in the text)

assumptions: The domain is Euclidean (or a grid) carrying the translation group, whose eigenfunctions are the Fourier basis.
The convolution and cross-correlation forms are interchangeable here because the filter is learnable.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The theorem is tied to translation structure; on general domains the Fourier basis is replaced by the Laplacian eigenbasis, which depends on the domain itself and behaves unstably across domains.

layer2.mapping: Spectral features in the engine are computed as products in a transform domain only where a genuine translation structure exists, namely regular time grids and field grids; elsewhere the engine uses spatial aggregation instead of pretending a spectrum exists.
layer2.telemetry: Periodic grid signals; sampling rates; transform-domain feature magnitudes.

primitives.name: Localised multiscale (wavelet) representations are approximately equivariant to deformations, where the Fourier modulus is unstable at O(1)
primitives.verbatim_quote: In other words, decomposing the signal information into scales using localised filters rather than frequencies turns a global unstable representation into a family of locally stable features.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.W_psi: wavelet transform with mother wavelet psi
symbol_and_unit_ledger.tau: deformation with sup_u ||grad tau(u)|| bounded by epsilon
symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(tau): action of the deformation on signals

assumptions: The deformation is close to a shift, with gradient sup-norm at most epsilon.
Wavelet atoms are localised in both space and frequency, sampled at dyadic scales.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Wavelet measurements are stable but not yet invariant; invariance must still be built by progressively processing toward low frequencies, and the Fourier modulus counterexample shows global spectral invariants fail at O(1) no matter how small epsilon is.

layer2.mapping: Engine spatial and temporal features are built from localised multiscale atoms rather than global spectra, so a local perturbation of the input perturbs features locally and proportionally instead of corrupting every coefficient at once.
layer2.telemetry: Multiscale feature pyramids; local perturbation response curves.

primitives.name: Scale separation prior: a locally stable function factorises as f approximately f_j after P_j through a hierarchy of coarsened domains
primitives.verbatim_quote: we informally say that a function f : X (Ω) → Y is locally stable at scale j if it admits a factorisation of the form f ≈ fj ◦ Pj , where Pj : X (Ω) → Xj (Ωj ) is a non-linear coarse graining and fj : Xj (Ωj ) → Y.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.f: target function on signals over Omega
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_j: nonlinear coarse-graining map X(Omega) to X_j(Omega_j)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.f_j: function defined on the coarsened domain at scale j

assumptions: The domain carries a metric so that nearby points can be assimilated by coarsening.
Long-range interactions of the target function separate across scales: local interactions are computed first and propagated to coarse scales.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Sets admit no predefined metric and hence no nontrivial coarsening, and target functions with genuinely global, non-separating interactions break the factorisation; stability alone (eq. 4) is not sufficient to beat the curse of dimensionality as domain size grows.

layer2.mapping: The engine organises inference hierarchically: fine-grained local interactions are computed first and summarised upward through coarser situation summaries, so long-range conclusions are compositions of local evidence rather than direct global fits.
layer2.telemetry: Hierarchy levels per signal; coarsening ratios; per-scale feature summaries.

primitives.name: The GDL blueprint: local equivariant layer, elementwise nonlinearity, coarsening, and a global invariant layer, composed as f = A o sigma_J o B_J o P_{J-1} ... P_1 o sigma_1 o B_1
primitives.verbatim_quote: provides three key building blocks: (i) a local equivariant map, (ii) a global invariant map, and (iii) a coarsening operator.
primitives.latex: f = A \circ \sigma_J \circ B_J \circ P_{J-1} \circ \cdots \circ P_1 \circ \sigma_1 \circ B_1

symbol_and_unit_ledger.A: G-invariant layer (global pooling) to the output space Y
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P_j: local pooling (coarsening) operators onto smaller domains

assumptions: The domain Omega carries a symmetry group G and, for locality and coarsening, a distance metric d.
Blocks are composed so that the output space of each block matches the input space of the next; different blocks may exploit different symmetry groups.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The blueprint states necessary building blocks rather than a unique architecture, and on domains without a metric (sets) localised maps and coarsening are unavailable, so only part of the template applies.

layer2.mapping: This composition is the engine's architecture template: local equivariant updates, pointwise nonlinear scoring, hierarchical coarsening of situations, and a single invariant readout at the end; any proposed module must identify which of the four blocks it implements.
layer2.telemetry: Module inventory mapped to blueprint blocks; group declaration per block.

primitives.name: Deep Sets form: permutation-invariant functions on sets are phi of a sum of per-element psi transforms
primitives.verbatim_quote: where the function ψ is independently applied to every node’s features, and φ is applied on its sum-aggregated outputs: as sum is independent of the order in which its inputs are provided, such a function is invariant with respect to the permutation of the node set

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: matrix stacking the element features x_u as rows
symbol_and_unit_ledger.psi: shared function applied independently to each element's features
symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi: function applied to the sum-aggregated output

assumptions: The input is a set: a graph with empty edge set, so elements have no relations.
Summation is the order-independent aggregator that makes the construction invariant.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Ignoring edges is equivalently expressive to ignoring all interaction terms: when a latent relational structure exists, the empty-edge-set model is representationally inferior, which motivates attentional and latent-graph variants.

layer2.mapping: Where the engine faces genuinely unordered collections, such as a pool of candidate plays or a roster, it uses the shared-transform-plus-sum form, guaranteeing the output cannot depend on the arbitrary order in which the collection happened to be listed.
layer2.telemetry: Unordered collection inputs; listing-order permutation tests.

primitives.name: Graph functions must be permutation invariant, f(PX, PAP^T) = f(X, A); isomorphic graphs yield identical outputs
primitives.verbatim_quote: The desirable property that functions acting on graphs should satisfy is thus permutation invariance, and it implies that for any two isomorphic graphs, the outcomes of these functions are identical.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: n x d node feature matrix

assumptions: Nodes are not provided in any canonical order.
Permuting node features with P automatically permutes the adjacency rows and columns with P A P^T, keeping features and structure synchronised.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The same invariance caps expressivity: invariant functions cannot distinguish any pair of isomorphic graphs, and neighbourhood-aggregating constructions inherit the Weisfeiler-Lehman limits described in Section 7.

layer2.mapping: Every graph-level engine output is invariant under node relabelling by construction and by test: the same matchup graph entered with entities listed in a different order returns identical conclusions.
layer2.telemetry: Relabelling consistency tests on matchup graphs; canonical ordering logs.

primitives.name: Blueprint recipe for graphs: a permutation-equivariant layer applies one shared local function phi(x_u, X_{N_u}) to every node and its neighbourhood multiset
primitives.verbatim_quote: The GDL blueprint thus yields a general recipe for constructing permutation equivariant functions on graphs, by specifying a local function φ that operates over the features of a node and its neighbourhood, φ(xu , XNu ).

symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi: shared local function, itself permutation invariant over the neighbourhood
symbol_and_unit_ledger.N_u: 1-hop neighbourhood {v : (u, v) in E or (v, u) in E}

assumptions: Locality on graphs is defined by the shortest-path distance.
Equivariance of F rests entirely on phi being independent of the ordering of nodes inside the neighbourhood.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When phi is injective the construction equals one Weisfeiler-Lehman refinement step, and when it is not injective the layer is strictly weaker; a single layer sees only 1-hop interactions, so long-range structure needs composition of layers.

layer2.mapping: Matchup and interaction reasoning in the engine is implemented as shared local updates over entity neighbourhoods: the same update rule applies to every entity and only the neighbourhood evidence differs, which keeps reasoning uniform across games, opponents and eras.
layer2.telemetry: Neighbourhood definitions per graph type; per-node update traces.

primitives.name: Convolution is derived, not invented: a linear map commutes with the shift operator if and only if it is a circulant convolution
primitives.verbatim_quote: This, in turn, allows us to define convolution as a translation equivariant linear operation, and is a nice illustration of the power of geometric priors and the overall philosophy of Geometric ML: convolution emerges from the first principle of translational symmetry.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C(theta): circulant matrix built from filter theta
symbol_and_unit_ledger.theta: filter coefficients, one degree of freedom per diagonal

assumptions: Periodic boundary conditions turn the 1D grid into a ring graph.
The symmetry group is the Abelian translation group, whose operators mutually commute.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The equivalence relies on the grid's fixed node ordering and homogeneous connectivity; on general graphs neighbours have no canonical order, so the characterisation of equivariant maps is entirely different (fifteen generators for graph signals).

layer2.mapping: The engine derives its operators from declared symmetries in the same direction: an operator is admitted only after the symmetry it must commute with is named, so weight sharing is a theorem about the domain rather than a heuristic.
layer2.telemetry: Symmetry declarations per operator; commutation tests.

primitives.name: Group convolution: match the signal against every group-transformed copy of the filter; the output is a function on the group itself
primitives.verbatim_quote: Note that x ? θ takes values on the elements g of our group G rather than points on the domain Ω.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho(g): representation of g acting on signals and filters
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Omega: domain equipped with an invariant measure

assumptions: Signals form a Hilbert space with inner product given by integration against an invariant measure.
For stacked layers the construction is applied with the group itself as domain (regular representation), since the convolution output lives on G.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Convolution requires integrating over the domain, so it is practical only for small or low-dimensional groups and domains: the permutation group Sigma_n has n! elements and the six-dimensional affine group is already infeasible, forcing work on low-dimensional spaces the group acts on.

layer2.mapping: When a signal's natural transformations go beyond translation, for example rotations or reflections of a spatial pattern, the engine lifts features over the transformation set itself, producing transformation-indexed features instead of collapsing them prematurely into a single map.
layer2.telemetry: Transformation-indexed feature stacks; group sizes per domain.

primitives.name: Homogeneous space: the group action is transitive, every point can be reached from every other, so all points look the same
primitives.verbatim_quote: whether Ω was a grid, plane, or the sphere, we could transform every point into any other point, intuitively meaning that all the points on the domain “look the same.”
primitives.latex: \forall\, u, v \in \Omega\ \exists\, g \in G :\ g \cdot u = v

symbol_and_unit_ledger.g.u: action of g on the point u

assumptions: The group action satisfies e.u = u and g.(h.u) = (gh).u.
Transitivity is what licenses sliding one shared filter across the whole domain.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Most manifolds are not homogeneous and carry no global symmetry group; transitivity fails there, a shared filter cannot be slid around, and intrinsic or gauge constructions must replace group convolution.

layer2.mapping: The engine checks homogeneity before sharing parameters across positions: parameters are shared only across positions the symmetry group can actually reach from one another, and position-specific parameters are used where transitivity fails.
layer2.telemetry: Position reachability under declared groups; parameter-sharing maps.

primitives.name: Intrinsic constructions, expressed only through the Riemannian metric, are automatically invariant to isometric deformation
primitives.verbatim_quote: If such functions can be expressed in terms of intrinsic quantities, they are automatically guaranteed to be isometry-invariant and thus unaffected by isometric deformations.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.d_g, d_h: geodesic distances induced by the metrics g and h
symbol_and_unit_ledger.eta: isometry (diffeomorphism with eta^* h = g) between the two manifolds

assumptions: The quantities used are expressible entirely in terms of the metric (geodesic distances, gradient, divergence, Laplacian).
Deformations considered are isometries, or near-isometries handled by the domain-deformation stability bound with distortion dis(eta).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Extrinsic information (how the surface sits in ambient space) is invisible to intrinsic features by design, and for merely approximate isometries the guarantee degrades from equality to the stability inequality governed by metric distortion.

layer2.mapping: Engine features that must survive re-representation are built from intrinsic quantities only, namely relations and distances internal to the situation, so re-embedding the same situation in a different presentation cannot change the conclusion drawn from them.
layer2.telemetry: Intrinsic feature inventory; re-presentation consistency tests.

primitives.name: Spectral convolution on manifolds: filter in the Laplacian eigenbasis, (x * theta)(u) = sum_k (x-hat_k theta-hat_k) phi_k(u), intrinsic by construction
primitives.verbatim_quote: By virtue of its construction, the spectral convolution is intrinsic and thus isometry-invariant.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.phi_k: eigenfunctions of the Laplace-Beltrami operator, Delta phi_k = lambda_k phi_k
symbol_and_unit_ledger.lambda_k: eigenvalues, the generalised frequencies, 0 = lambda_0 <= lambda_1 <= ...
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x-hat_k: Fourier coefficients <x, phi_k> of the signal

assumptions: The manifold is compact, so the Laplacian spectrum is discrete and the eigenfunctions form an orthogonal basis.
The Laplacian eigenbasis is optimal for representing smooth signals: no other basis attains a better truncation error.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The Laplacian is isotropic, so spectral filters have no sense of direction, and direct evaluation needs the eigendecomposition; worse, the basis itself is unstable under domain perturbation (next primitive), which is why transfer-function filters replace it in practice.

layer2.mapping: Where the engine uses spectral summaries of one fixed structure, it uses transforms of that structure's own Laplacian and treats the spectrum as a fingerprint of that fixed domain only, never as a transferable coordinate system.
layer2.telemetry: Per-domain Laplacian spectra; spectral feature vectors with domain identifiers.

primitives.name: Spectral bases are geometrically unstable: high-frequency Laplacian eigenfunctions change dramatically under small near-isometric perturbations of the domain
primitives.verbatim_quote: Even worse, it turns out geometrically unstable: the higher-frequency eigenfunctions of the Laplacian can change dramatically as a result of even small near-isometric perturbations of the domain Ω (see Figure 12).
assumptions: Perturbations are near-isometric but nonzero.
The filter depends on individual eigenfunctions rather than on a function of the eigenvalues.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Low-frequency eigenfunctions are comparatively stable, and filters expressed as transfer functions p-hat(Delta) of the Laplacian are provably stable under approximate isometries; the failure is a property of basis-dependent filters, not of spectral methods as such.

layer2.mapping: The engine never transfers a basis-dependent representation from one domain to another: a feature defined through one graph's eigenvectors is quarantined to that graph, and any cross-domain claim must be rebuilt from transferable quantities.
layer2.telemetry: Domain identifiers attached to spectral features; cross-domain usage blocks.

primitives.name: Polynomial filters in the Laplacian (ChebNet construction): p-hat(Delta) X = sum_k alpha_k Delta^k X, localised in r hops and free of eigendecomposition
primitives.verbatim_quote: Defferrard et al. (2016) used polynomials of degree r as filter functions

symbol_and_unit_ledger.p-hat: spectral transfer function applied to the Laplacian
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Delta: Laplacian matrix, sparse with O(|E|) nonzeros
symbol_and_unit_ledger.r: polynomial degree, equal to the filter's hop radius
symbol_and_unit_ledger.X: n x d node feature matrix

assumptions: The Laplacian is local (1-hop), so Delta^k reaches exactly k-hop neighbourhoods.
Computation is by repeated sparse matrix multiplication, with complexity O(|E| d r), avoiding the O(n^3) eigendecomposition.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A degree-r polynomial's physical support depends on mesh resolution, so the same filter covers different areas on fine and coarse discretisations of one surface; resolution-independent filtering needs rational (Cayley) filters, which have exponential rather than compact support but are stable under approximate isometric deformation.

layer2.mapping: Diffusion-style features in the engine are computed as short polynomial diffusions over the interaction graph, which bounds how far evidence can travel and makes every feature's receptive field explicit and auditable.
layer2.telemetry: Diffusion depths per feature; graph sparsity statistics.

primitives.name: Gauge equivariance: a layer must satisfy f o rho_in(g) = rho_out(g) o f, so its coordinate expression is independent of the arbitrary local frame
primitives.verbatim_quote: In other words, the coordinate expression of a gauge equivariant map is independent of the gauge, in the same way that in the case of graph, we applied the same function regardless of how the input nodes were permuted.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.rho_in, rho_out: representations of the structure group G on the input and output fibres
symbol_and_unit_ledger.g: gauge transformation, a map Omega to G acting independently at each point

assumptions: Features are sections of a bundle whose fibres carry representations of the structure group (e.g. SO(2) for tangent frames).
Comparing features at different points requires parallel transporters rho(g_{v to u}) along the connecting geodesic, precomputable per mesh.
primitives.breakdown_regime: A smooth global gauge may not exist at all (the sphere is not parallelisable), filters between points must be transported, and the kernel constraint Theta rho(g) = rho(g) Theta restricts the learnable filter space to a subspace spanned by basis kernels.

layer2.mapping: Engine features that depend on a local reference choice, such as a chosen orientation for a formation or a chosen baseline for a rating, must be provably independent of that choice, or the dependence must be declared as part of the feature; silent frame dependence is treated as a defect.
layer2.telemetry: Frame-dependence audits; reference-choice sensitivity tests.

primitives.name: Cotangent Laplacian: the mesh discretisation of Laplace-Beltrami with weights w_uv = (cot angle uqv + cot angle upv) / (2 a_u), intrinsic and convergent under refinement
primitives.verbatim_quote: The cotangent Laplacian can be shown to have multiple convenient properties (see e.g. Wardetzky et al. (2007)): it is a positive-semidefinite matrix

symbol_and_unit_ledger.w_uv: Laplacian weight on edge (u, v) in (Delta X)_u = sum_v w_uv (x_u - x_v)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.angle uqv, angle upv: angles opposite the shared edge (u, v) in its two incident triangles
symbol_and_unit_ledger.a_u: local area element at node u (mixed Voronoi area)

assumptions: The mesh is a manifold triangular mesh: each edge is shared by exactly two triangles and node neighbourhoods are disk-like.
Mesh refinement is non-degenerate, avoiding pathological triangulations such as the Schwarz lantern.
primitives.breakdown_regime: The weights can be rewritten purely in terms of edge lengths, which is what makes the operator intrinsic; on non-manifold meshes or degenerate triangulations the convergence to the continuous Laplace-Beltrami operator fails, and the combinatorial Laplacian (weights from adjacency only) remains available but carries no geometry.

layer2.mapping: When the engine discretises a continuous structure, such as field geometry or a spatial influence surface, edge weights are derived from the geometry of the discretisation itself rather than set uniformly, so finer structure carries correctly weighted influence.
layer2.telemetry: Geometry-derived edge weights; discretisation resolution per surface.

primitives.name: Three GNN flavours under strict representational containment: convolution (fixed weights) inside attention (learned scalars) inside message passing (learned vectors)
primitives.verbatim_quote: One important thing to note is a representational containment between these approaches: convolution ⊆ attention ⊆ message-passing.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.c_uv: fixed importance weight of neighbour v for u, from the graph structure (convolutional flavour)

assumptions: All three flavours aggregate the neighbourhood with a permutation-invariant aggregator and update with a shared function phi.

Containment is representational: attention reduces to convolution when a is a lookup table c_uv, and both reduce to message passing with messages psi(x_u, x_v) = c_uv psi(x_v) or a(x_u, x_v) psi(x_v).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Containment is not a ranking of usefulness: message passing is harder to train and memory-hungry, while on homophilous graphs (edges signalling same-class neighbours) convolutional aggregation is often the better regularised and more scalable choice, with attention as the middle ground.

layer2.mapping: The engine selects the weakest flavour that expresses the needed interaction: fixed-weight aggregation where structure already encodes relevance, scalar attention where relevance must be inferred, and full vector messages only where vector-valued interaction is genuinely required.
layer2.telemetry: Per-layer flavour choice; edge weight provenance (fixed versus learned).

primitives.name: Transformers are attentional GNNs over a complete graph: self-attention infers a soft adjacency matrix a_uv = a(x_u, x_v)
primitives.verbatim_quote: we can constrain all the scalars a(xu , xv ) to be in the range [0, 1]; as such, we can think of self-attention as inferring a soft adjacency matrix, auv = a(xu , xv )

symbol_and_unit_ledger.a_uv: soft adjacency (attention) coefficient between elements u and v, normalised into [0, 1]
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_u, x_v: feature vectors of elements u and v
symbol_and_unit_ledger.V: the full element set, since the graph is complete (N_u = V)

assumptions: No adjacency is given, so the complete graph is assumed and no pair of elements is excluded in advance.
Positional encodings reintroduce sequence (grid) structure, and can themselves be read as Laplacian eigenvectors of a circular grid.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Complete-graph attention costs quadratic memory in the number of elements, and with no positional information the model cannot represent order at all; inferring a general latent adjacency instead is a hard discrete structure-learning problem.

layer2.mapping: For unstructured collections where relations are unknown, the engine lets attention infer a soft relational graph as a byproduct of training, and that inferred graph is itself logged as evidence about which entities the model believes interact.
layer2.telemetry: Inferred attention graphs per input; attention entropy statistics.

primitives.name: Weisfeiler-Lehman ceiling: no GNN of the three flavours can be more powerful than the WL graph isomorphism test
primitives.verbatim_quote: one of the three flavours we outlined in Section 5.3 cannot be more powerful than the WL test!
assumptions: The GNN conforms to one of the three flavours with permutation-invariant neighbourhood aggregation.
Xu et al. (2018): the ceiling is attained only when the aggregation and update functions are injective (the GIN condition).
primitives.breakdown_regime: The ceiling binds only inside the class: higher-order networks from the Weisfeiler-Lehman hierarchy, explicit spectral or structural features, and random or identifier features escape it at real computational cost; a concrete failure pair is the 6-cycle versus two disjoint triangles.

layer2.mapping: Engine capability claims are capped by this ceiling: before a relational question is assigned to a graph model, it is checked whether colour refinement could separate the structures at all, and questions above the ceiling are routed to richer representations instead of larger training runs.
layer2.telemetry: WL-separability pre-checks per task; escalation records to higher-order features.

primitives.name: E(3)-equivariant message passing (EGNN): features update only through squared distances, coordinates update along relative position vectors
primitives.verbatim_quote: This is due to the fact that the only dependence of fu0 on xu is through the distances kxu − xv k2 , and the action of E(3) necessarily leaves distances between nodes unchanged.
primitives.latex: x'_u = x_u + \sum_{v \ne u} (x_u - x_v)\,\psi_c(f_u, f_v, \|x_u - x_v\|^2)

symbol_and_unit_ledger.x_u: spatial coordinates of node u in R^3
symbol_and_unit_ledger.psi_f: learnable feature message function in the companion feature update
symbol_and_unit_ledger.||x_u - x_v||^2: squared Euclidean distance, invariant under E(3)

assumptions: Node inputs split into coordinates transforming under the Euclidean group E(3) (rho(g)x = R x + b) and features f that must stay invariant.
The only coordinate dependence of the feature update is through pairwise distances, which E(3) leaves unchanged.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Scalar features cannot encode directional quantities such as velocities except through extensions; features transforming as general tensors require irreducible representation machinery (Tensor Field Networks, SE(3)-Transformers) or regular representations (LieConv), beyond this layer.

layer2.mapping: Spatial reasoning in the engine keeps coordinates and properties separate: property updates depend only on invariant relations such as distances, and coordinate-like quantities are updated along relative directions, so rotating or translating the whole scene cannot change the verdict.
layer2.telemetry: Distance and angle feature tables; rotation and translation consistency tests.

primitives.name: LSTM: a persistent memory cell whose state is gated in, retained and gated out, c(t) = i(t) c-tilde(t) + f(t) c(t-1), h(t) = o(t) tanh(c(t))
primitives.verbatim_quote: The LSTM augments the recurrent computation by introducing a memory cell, which stores cell state vectors, c(t) ∈ Rm , that are preserved between computational steps.
primitives.latex: c^{(t)} = i^{(t)} \odot \tilde{c}^{(t)} + f^{(t)} \odot c^{(t-1)}, \qquad h^{(t)} = o^{(t)} \odot \tanh(c^{(t)})

symbol_and_unit_ledger.c(t): cell state vector at step t, in R^m
symbol_and_unit_ledger.c-tilde(t): candidate features tanh(W_c z(t) + U_c h(t-1) + b_c)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.i(t), f(t), o(t): input, forget and output gate vectors with values in [0, 1]^m, computed with the logistic sigmoid

assumptions: All three gates are computed from the current input z(t) and the previous summary h(t-1) by single fully connected layers.
The cell state reaches the output only through the output gate and tanh, and reaches the next step additively, which is what controls gradient vanishing.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Gating mitigates but does not abolish vanishing and exploding gradients, and the fixed-size summary h(T) remains a representational bottleneck for long sequences, the pressure that recurrent attention and then Transformers were introduced to relieve.

layer2.mapping: Engine sequence modules keep an explicit gated carry state for long-range context, such as a game's evolving state or a season-long narrative, where what is retained, overwritten, or emitted is a learned per-dimension decision rather than a fixed decay.
layer2.telemetry: Gate activation statistics; carry-state horizon measurements.

primitives.name: Functional maps: correspondence between two domains as a linear operator C between their function spaces, with operators transporting as Q' = C Q C^T
primitives.verbatim_quote: replacing the correspondence between points on two domains (a map η : Ω → Ω0 ) with correspondence between functions (a map C : X (Ω) → X (Ω0 ), see Figure 13)
primitives.latex: x' = Cx, \qquad Q' = C Q C^\top

symbol_and_unit_ledger.C: functional map, an n' x n matrix (implemented as a small k x k map between truncated Laplacian eigenbases)
symbol_and_unit_ledger.x, x': signals on the first and second domains
symbol_and_unit_ledger.Q, Q': operator (e.g. Laplacian) representations of the two meshes
symbol_and_unit_ledger.P: permutation matrices are the special case C in O(n) with C^{-1} = C^T

assumptions: The two meshes discretise the same underlying continuous surface but may differ in connectivity and even in node count.
Area-preserving maps are exactly the orthogonal functional maps, C^T C = I (Rustamov et al. 2013).
primitives.breakdown_regime: Pointwise correspondences cannot even be stated when node counts differ, the functional map must be estimated (typically spectrally), and remeshing-invariant functions are forced to depend on the operator only through its spectrum, f(Q) = f(Lambda).

layer2.mapping: Cross-domain alignment in the engine is done in function space: instead of forcing a one-to-one matching between entities of two datasets, signals and operators are transported through a linear map, and transported operators must satisfy Q' = C Q C^T as a consistency check.
layer2.telemetry: Functional map matrices between dataset versions; transport consistency residuals.

primitives.name: Gates are forced by time-warping invariance: a warp-invariant RNN must have the gated form, with the gate Gamma fitting the warping derivative d tau/dt
primitives.verbatim_quote: Achieving time warping invariance is tightly coupled with presence of gating mechanisms, such as the input/forget/output gates of LSTMs.

symbol_and_unit_ledger.Gamma: learnable gate in (0, 1) approximating the warping derivative d tau/dt

assumptions: Warping tau is monotone increasing and differentiable, and non-destructive: dilations are allowed, contractions are limited by d tau/dt near or below 1 for the Taylor argument.
Class invariance is required: for every warping there exists a model in the class processing warped data identically, not the same parameters.
primitives.breakdown_regime: SimpleRNNs are exactly the degenerate case Gamma = 1 (no warping assumed) and so cannot be warp-invariant; destructive contractions that skip intermediate data defeat any gate, and trained gates do not transfer zero-shot between different warpings except under pure rescaling, where gates rescale by the same factor.

layer2.mapping: Tempo variation in engine time series, such as pace changes or compressed schedules, is modelled as time warping, and gated modules are initialised with chrono initialisation so their forgetting horizons, proportional to 1/Gamma, cover the range of tempos the data actually contains.
layer2.telemetry: Tempo and warp statistics per series; gate horizon coverage versus required range.

reasoning_traces.think: This text is the founding blueprint of geometric deep learning, written by Bronstein, Bruna, Cohen and Velickovic in 2021, and its central move is to treat architecture design as applied geometry rather than as engineering folklore. The argument starts from a negative result: learning generic functions in high dimensions is cursed, because even the mildest smoothness class, the 1-Lipschitz functions, needs a number of samples exponential in the dimension before any estimator can be trusted. Real tasks are learnable only because the target functions are not generic. They carry regularity that comes from the physical world, and the text names the two master regularities as symmetry and scale separation. Everything else in the book is machinery for turning those two words into layer equations. The first machine is group theory. A symmetry is a transformation that leaves a property unchanged; symmetries compose and invert, so they form a group; groups act on domains, and the action lifts to signals through representations, matrix-valued homomorphisms satisfying rho(gh) = rho(g)rho(h). Once that language exists, the two central definitions fall out immediately. A function is invariant if the group action on its input does not change its output, and equivariant if the action passes through to the output. These two definitions explain, retroactively, why multilayer perceptrons failed at vision and why convolutional layers are shift equivariant rather than shift invariant, and they become design constraints: any layer an architect writes down can be audited by asking which group it respects and whether it respects it exactly. The second machine softens exact symmetry into stability. Real deformations are not group elements, because small deformations compose into large ones and break closure, so the text replaces invariance with a Lipschitz-style bound: the output may move, but at most in proportion to a deformation cost that vanishes exactly on the symmetry subgroup. The same idea is then lifted from signals to domains, with distances between domains defined by the best structure-preserving alignment, which is how graph edit distance and Gromov-Hausdorff distance enter the story. Scale separation completes the prior stack: a locally stable function factorises through a hierarchy of coarsened domains, so long-range interaction is built by composing local operations across scales instead of being learned globally at once. The contrast between Fourier and wavelet representations is the cautionary tale here: a global spectral basis is exactly equivariant but unstable under small deformations, while localised multiscale atoms trade exactness for stability. The blueprint then assembles everything into four blocks, a linear equivariant layer, an elementwise nonlinearity, a local pooling or coarsening operator, and a global invariant pooling, composed with pooling interleaved between the equivariant layers. Any architecture in the book, and by the authors' claim most architectures in use, is an instantiation of that composition for a specific domain and group. The five domains are where the blueprint earns its keep. Sets and graphs carry the permutation group, and the local construction, apply one shared permutation-invariant function to each node and its neighbourhood multiset, yields message passing and, with an injective local function, exactly one Weisfeiler-Lehman refinement step. Grids carry translations, and the derivation runs backwards from symmetry to architecture: a linear map commutes with the shift operator if and only if it is a circulant matrix, so convolution is not an invention but the unique answer to translation equivariance, and the Fourier basis is forced as the joint eigenbasis of all circulants. Groups and homogeneous spaces generalise this to group convolution, where the filter is matched against every group-transformed copy of itself and the output lives on the group, which is why spherical convolution outputs a function on SO(3) rather than on the sphere. Manifolds break the pattern, because they usually have no global symmetry group at all; the surviving structure is intrinsic, meaning expressible through the Riemannian metric alone, and intrinsic constructions are automatically isometry invariant. The Laplace-Beltrami operator supplies a Fourier basis, but the text is honest about the price: high-frequency eigenfunctions are unstable under small perturbations of the domain, so spectral filters are only safe when expressed as functions of the Laplacian, such as polynomials, which are automatically local and avoid diagonalisation. Gauges push one level deeper: features on a manifold are only defined relative to a local frame, the frame choice is arbitrary, and demanding that a layer's coordinate expression be independent of that choice yields gauge equivariance, with parallel transport used to compare vectors living in different tangent spaces before any filter is applied. Meshes discretise all of this, with the cotangent Laplacian as the workhorse that converges to the continuous operator and depends only on edge lengths. The model chapters then read as corollaries. CNNs are the blueprint on grids, down to residual connections being reinterpreted as Euler steps of an ordinary differential equation. Group-equivariant CNNs implement group convolution by transforming filters and reusing ordinary convolution. GNNs collapse into three flavours with a strict containment, convolution inside attention inside message passing, and Transformers are recovered as attentional GNNs on a complete graph whose self-attention coefficients form a learned soft adjacency. Equivariant message passing handles coordinates by feeding only invariant distances into the feature update and letting coordinate updates be weighted sums of relative position vectors, which is exactly equivariant under rigid motions. Gauge-equivariant mesh CNNs implement the transported filter equation as message passing with precomputed transporter matrices. Recurrent networks close the book with a temporal symmetry: requiring class invariance to time warping forces the update to contain a multiplicative gate in the unit interval, which is precisely the LSTM gate structure, and the forget-gate bias initialisation known as chrono initialisation follows from choosing which range of time horizons the gate should cover. For a reasoning engine, the transferable lesson is discipline about structure. Every signal should be declared with its domain and its symmetry group, every operator should state whether it is invariant, equivariant, or merely stable, and every claimed correspondence between two domains should be checked as a map between functions, not just points. The text also supplies its own warning labels: permutation-invariant local aggregation cannot distinguish some non-isomorphic graphs, spectral bases do not transfer across domains, and gauge choices can silently contaminate features near singularities. A system that internalises both the constructions and the failure modes gets a principled way to build new layers for new domains instead of a catalogue of architectures to imitate.
reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: The lineage runs from Klein's Erlangen Programme, which defined a geometry by the invariants of its transformation group, through Weyl's writings on symmetry and the classical harmonic analysis of Fourier, into Mallat's wavelets and scattering stability theory and the spectral geometry of the Laplace-Beltrami operator. The deep learning branch grows from Fukushima's Neocognitron and LeCun's convolutional networks, through Bruna's spectral graph networks of 2013, Cohen and Welling's group equivariant convolutions, and the message passing synthesis of Gilmer et al. and Battaglia et al., while Weisfeiler and Lehman's 1968 colour refinement test supplies the expressivity yardstick the graph branch still measures itself against. The recurrent branch descends from Hochreiter and Schmidhuber's 1997 LSTM, reinterpreted by Tallec and Ollivier in 2018 as a time-warping invariance mechanism.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: The authors model their reader as a practitioner who knows the architectures by name but has never seen them derived, and who is suspected of treating convolution, pooling, attention and recurrence as unrelated inventions. Their wager is that this reader actually wants a generative grammar: given a new domain, they want to know which group acts on it, what locality means there, and which layer equations are then forced. The authors also model the domain itself as honest: physical data is assumed to be generated by processes with real symmetries and real multiscale structure, so the geometry is discovered in the problem rather than imposed on it. Rigor is used as persuasion; every architecture is earned by a derivation, never merely announced.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: Several results in the text veto naive designs in other layers. The Weisfeiler-Lehman ceiling vetoes any claim that a standard message passing layer can separate graph structures that colour refinement cannot, no matter how long it is trained. The instability of high-frequency Laplacian eigenfunctions vetoes transferring spectral filters across different domains, so a spectral layer validated on one mesh is not evidence about another. The deformation stability bound vetoes demanding exact invariance where only stability is achievable, and the gauge analysis vetoes any feature that depends on an arbitrary local frame choice, because such a feature changes when the frame changes even though the underlying object did not. Depth cannot repeal any of these vetoes; they are properties of the domain, not of the optimiser.

universal_lens: Read generally, the text is a method for attacking any structured prediction problem: name the domain your objects live on, name the transformations that must not matter, demand that each processing step either preserve those transformations or degrade provably gracefully under them, and organise computation from local interactions toward global summaries across scales. The same template organises problems far from learning, including simulation, compression, and correspondence between representations, because in each case the hard part is deciding what equivalence means and then refusing to let any component silently break it.
gsi_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Institute, the work supplies a research grammar for studying sport as structured data. A season, a play sequence, a formation, or a matchup graph each has a domain and a symmetry group: relabelling players, mirroring the field, or reordering equivalent plays should not change an analysis, while genuinely different structures must remain distinguishable. The stability results justify comparing across seasons and rule changes as approximate isometries rather than identical domains, and the expressivity ceiling warns the Institute which relational questions a given model class cannot answer in principle, before any data is collected or any conclusion is published.
gse_mapping: For the Galaxy Sports Edge reasoning engine, the blueprint becomes an audit checklist for every signal and operator. Each input feed is declared with its domain, whether that is a set of players, a graph of matchups, a grid of field positions, or a time series of game states, together with the transformations it must respect. Layers that aggregate neighbourhoods are built to be permutation equivariant by construction, global summaries are formed only by invariant pooling, and temporal modules use gating so that changes in game tempo act as time warping rather than as new information. Signals that fail a symmetry audit are flagged as unstable features instead of being silently trusted.
